days.title: Courage Rooted in God’s Presence and Promises
days.scripture_text: Have I not commanded you? Be strong and courageous. Do not be afraid; do not be discouraged, for the LORD your God will be with you wherever you go.
days.context:
God had already promised the land to Abraham.
He told Abraham, “I will give this land to your offspring.” The promise was sure.
But the land was still occupied by strong pagan nations, and they were wicked.
To take possession of what God had already given them, Israel had to cross the Jordan and face the enemies.
Moses—the only leader the people had known for the last 40 years—had just died.
The people were watching and waiting. The task was heavy.

Into that moment God commanded Joshua:
“Be strong and courageous… for the LORD your God will be with you wherever you go.” (Joshua 1:9)
Joshua’s courage was about stepping into the future God had already promised.
Joshua was about to lead God’s people into the Promised Land.

Joshua was fearful. He may have felt:
• “I’m not Moses. How can I fill his shoes?”
• “What if the people reject me?”
• “The enemies look too strong, and they’re giants.”
• “What if I fail?”
• “I feel scared and discouraged.”
God kept telling him, “Be strong and courageous.”

God did not give Joshua a pep talk to try harder or believe in himself. He said:
“The LORD your God will be with you wherever you go.”
Grounded in the presence and promises of God, Joshua obeyed, trusted God, and led.
Recurring theme in Joshua: God is the one fighting for His people—“the LORD, the God of Israel, fought for Israel.” (Joshua 10:42)
days.deeper_text:
After the death of Moses the servant of the LORD, the LORD said to Joshua son of Nun, Moses’ aide: “Moses my servant is dead. Now then, you and all these people, get ready to cross the Jordan River into the land I am about to give to them—to the Israelites. I will give you every place where you set your foot, as I promised Moses. Your territory will extend from the desert to Lebanon, and from the great river, the Euphrates—all the Hittite country—to the Mediterranean Sea in the west. No one will be able to stand against you all the days of your life. As I was with Moses, so I will be with you; I will never leave you nor forsake you. Be strong and courageous, because you will lead these people to inherit the land I swore to their ancestors to give them.

“Be strong and very courageous. Be careful to obey all the law my servant Moses gave you; do not turn from it to the right or to the left, that you may be successful wherever you go. Keep this Book of the Law always on your lips; meditate on it day and night, so that you may be careful to do everything written in it. Then you will be prosperous and successful. Have I not commanded you? Be strong and courageous. Do not be afraid; do not be discouraged, for the LORD your God will be with you wherever you go.”
days.summary: Moses was gone. God had already promised the land to His people long before Joshua. God called Joshua to lead them into it. The task was huge—the land was occupied by seven fortified pagan nations, and the enemies were strong and wicked. God told Joshua to find courage not in himself but in two unshakable supernatural realities: the promise of the land and the promise of God’s presence in his life. The courage God required of Joshua is the courage to obey Him. This includes keeping and obeying the Book of the Law, God’s standards for His people to live by for success. Joshua’s courage was to step forward into what God had already given, trusting that He would be with Joshua every step of the way. Grounded in the presence and promises of God, Joshua obeyed, trusted God, and led. Recurring theme in Joshua: God is the one fighting for His people—“the LORD, the God of Israel, fought for Israel.” (Joshua 10:42)
days.upward:
Joshua’s courage started by looking up to God.
God did not say, “Be brave because you can do it.”
He said, “Be strong and courageous, because I am with you.”
Courage for you begins the same way: turning your eyes upward and trusting that God is actually with you in the place that feels too big.
upward_questions: When you face something that feels too big, what do you usually do first—try to handle it alone, avoid it, or turn to God?
days.inward:
Joshua had outside fears: the enemies, the huge task of leading God’s people. Joshua also had fears inside his heart: pressure, comparison, falling short, failing.
God’s presence was meant to assure his heart.
Your worth and security are not based on whether you are as strong as someone else, being spot on, or feeling brave.
It’s not about personal ability.
True courage stands on this truth: God is with you and He will never leave you.
inward_questions: Which of Joshua’s fears feels most like something you deal with right now? Why?
Have you ever felt pressure to measure up to someone else? How did that affect you?
days.outward:
Joshua could move forward into hard places because he made the courageous decision to obey God, grounded in God’s promise to be with him.
He could lead, obey, and trust God in the face of opposition without being ruled by fear.
Your courage is also meant to move outward—into school, friendships, family, and everyday choices—because God goes with you.
outward_questions: God told Joshua that courage comes from His presence, not from Joshua’s own strength. How is that different from the messages you usually hear about being strong or confident?
days.prayer:
God, You told Joshua to be strong and courageous because You were with him.
You know the places where I feel small, compared, scared, or not enough.
Help me trust that You are with me wherever I go.
Give me courage today to take the next faithful step to obey You. Amen.
self_application: Where do I feel most like Joshua today—facing something new, hard, or overwhelming?
What is one situation where I need to remember: “God is with me wherever I go”?
If I truly believed God was with me there, what would change in how I think or act?
days.love_in_action:
Choose one small act of courage today that shows love to someone else.
Speak encouragement, stand firm in God’s truth, include someone left out, or stay faithful in a hard situation.
love_in_action_questions: What is one small courageous step I can take this week, trusting that the God who was with Joshua is with me too?

days.title: Courage That Obeys God Rather Than Man
days.scripture_text: But Peter and the apostles answered, “We must obey God rather than men.”
days.context:
The apostles were witnesses to Jesus and His resurrection.
The apostles spoke about Jesus publicly, and many people were healed.
More and more people believed in Jesus.
Everyday people brought their sick and those with unclean spirits to the apostles.
The apostles healed them all.

The religious leaders were powerful and opposed to the apostles. They arrested the apostles and put them in jail.
But that night the angel of the Lord opened the jail doors and told them to speak in the temple courts about new life in Jesus. They did.
The next day the religious leaders found the jail empty and the apostles gone.
They found the apostles teaching about Jesus in the temple courts and brought them before the religious council.
The religious leaders ordered the apostles to stop teaching in Jesus’ name.

Peter and the other apostles said: “We must obey God rather than human beings!” (Acts 5:29)
This was not careless resistance; it was Spirit-led obedience.
Peter did not plead for mercy. Instead he proclaimed Jesus—in front of the highest religious council—as the risen Savior whom the religious leaders had killed.
This is courage rooted in confidence that God was with them, even in the face of the threat of another arrest, beating, or even death.
It was the steady decision to keep obeying God even when it cost them safety, reputation, and freedom.
days.deeper_text:
Then the high priest and all his associates, who were members of the party of the Sadducees, were filled with jealousy. They arrested the apostles and put them in the public jail. But during the night an angel of the Lord opened the doors of the jail and brought them out. “Go, stand in the temple courts,” he said, “and tell the people all about this new life.” At daybreak they entered the temple courts, as they had been told, and began to teach the people.

When the high priest and his associates arrived, they called together the Sanhedrin—the full assembly of the elders of Israel—and sent to the jail for the apostles. But on arriving at the jail, the officers did not find them there. So they went back and reported, “We found the jail securely locked, with the guards standing at the doors; but when we opened them, we found no one inside.” On hearing this report, the captain of the temple guard and the chief priests were at a loss, wondering what this might lead to. Then someone came and said, “Look! The men you put in jail are standing in the temple courts teaching the people.” At that, the captain went with his officers and brought the apostles. They did not use force, because they feared that the people would stone them.

The apostles were brought in and made to appear before the Sanhedrin to be questioned by the high priest. “We gave you strict orders not to teach in this name,” he said. “Yet you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching and are determined to make us guilty of this man’s blood.” Peter and the other apostles replied: “We must obey God rather than human beings! The God of our ancestors raised Jesus from the dead—whom you killed by hanging him on a cross. God exalted him to his own right hand as Prince and Savior that he might bring Israel to repentance and forgive their sins. We are witnesses of these things, and so is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey him.”
days.summary: The religious leaders arrested the apostles because they were jealous. They wanted to silence the apostles from speaking about Jesus. The courage of the apostles was not self-generated; it was Spirit-generated. The apostles’ courage was not the absence of fear. The apostles knew the cost—more arrests, beatings, or even death—yet they chose to keep speaking the truth God had given them rather than submit to a human command that contradicted God’s clear will. They feared God’s judgment rather than man’s approval. This is the courage that holds the principle of higher authority: when human authority demands actions that God forbids, or prevents actions that God commands, then it is our duty—“We must [not may] obey God rather than human beings!” God’s people must obey God.
days.upward:
Courage looks first to God.
When pressure comes from people—friends, teachers, leaders, or culture—the real question is not “What will they think?”
It is “What has God said?”
Peter and the apostles chose to obey God because they believed He was the higher authority.
upward_questions: When you feel pressure to go along with others, whose voice do you listen to first—God’s or people’s?
days.inward:
This kind of courage starts in the heart.
It means deciding that God’s approval matters more than being liked, accepted, or safe.
Fear of what others think can make us quiet when we should speak, or go along when we should stand.
God invites you to a deeper loyalty—one that begins inside.
inward_questions: Where do you feel the strongest pull to please people instead of obeying God?
What would it look like to value God’s voice more than that pressure?
days.outward:
Obedience to God shows up in real choices.
It may mean speaking truth kindly, refusing to join in what dishonors Him, or staying faithful when it costs something.
Peter and the apostles did not stop talking about Jesus. They kept going because obedience mattered more than comfort.
outward_questions: Is there one place in your life right now where obeying God would cost you something—reputation, ease, or acceptance?
days.prayer:
God, You are worthy of my obedience.
When people pressure me to go a different way, help me choose You.
Give me courage to obey You rather than men.
Make my heart loyal to You first. Amen.
self_application: Where do I feel pressure to please people more than God?
What is one clear thing God has said that I need to obey, even if it is hard?
If I chose to obey God in that place, what might it cost—and what would I gain?
days.love_in_action: Choose one small act of courage that shows love and obedience today: speak truth kindly, refuse to join what dishonors God, speak about Jesus to encourage someone, or stay faithful when it would be easier to go along.
love_in_action_questions: What is one small courageous step I can take this week, choosing to obey God rather than the pressure of people?

days.title: Courage That Stays at the Work
days.scripture_text:
I sent messengers to them with this reply: “I am carrying on a great project and cannot go down. Why should the work stop while I leave it and go down to you?”

But I said, “Should a man like me run away? Or should someone like me go into the temple to save his life? I will not go!”
days.context:
Jerusalem’s walls were broken. The gates were burned. The city was in ruins, in danger.
Nehemiah heard the report, wept, prayed, and then asked the king for permission to go rebuild.

When the work began, enemies rose up to stop it.
They mocked and taunted the builders.
Nehemiah turned to prayer.
It took courage for Nehemiah to stay silent and not fight back.

The enemies threatened military attack.
Nehemiah turned to prayer and posted guards around the clock—faith and action.
The builders were discouraged and close to quitting.
Nehemiah rallied and strengthened them.
He reminded them of the greatness of God—trust in God—and of who they were fighting for: their families.
This courage looked to God, not circumstances.
Result: the enemies retreated.

The enemies switched tactics and targeted Nehemiah.
They sent four invitations to get Nehemiah out to meet with them.
Each time Nehemiah said “no”—he knew this was a trap to harm him.
The enemies falsely accused Nehemiah of plotting to revolt against the Persian king—treason punishable by execution.
Nehemiah called out their lies and made-up stories.
He prayed that God would strengthen his hands.
He could have panicked or defended himself; instead he kept building.
Nehemiah’s trust in God was unshakable.

A prophet told Nehemiah to hide from the killers inside the temple.
Nehemiah said “no”—he would not run away or hide.
This was the courage to say “no” even when the advice came from a spiritual person.
Nehemiah realized this prophet was hired to intimidate him into sin—desecrating the temple—and to ruin his reputation.

The wall was completed in 52 days in the midst of heavy opposition.
Nehemiah’s courage came from a place of unshakable trust in God and obedience to Him.
days.deeper_text:
“Don’t be afraid of them. Remember the Lord, who is great and awesome, and fight for your families, your sons and your daughters, your wives and your homes… Those who carried materials did their work with one hand and held a weapon in the other.” (Nehemiah 4:14, 17)

“Sanballat and Geshem sent me this message: ‘Come, let us meet together…’ But they were scheming to harm me; so I sent messengers to them with this reply: ‘I am carrying on a great project and cannot go down. Why should the work stop while I leave it and go down to you?’ …I realized that God had not sent him, but that he had prophesied against me because Tobiah and Sanballat had hired him… But I said, ‘Should a man like me run away? Or should someone like me go into the temple to save his life? I will not go!’ … So the wall was completed… in fifty-two days. When all our enemies heard about this, all the surrounding nations were afraid and lost their self-confidence, because they realized that this work had been done with the help of our God.” (Nehemiah 6:2-3, 12, 11, 15-16)
days.summary: Nehemiah rebuilt Jerusalem’s walls under mockery, threat, and trap. The enemies tried to stop the work by breaking down the builders’ spirit through fear. Nehemiah prayed, posted guards, kept building, and refused both to meet with the enemies and to hide from them—either would have taken his focus off the wall. His courage didn’t happen overnight—it was obedience under pressure over a long stretch of time. The wall was finished in 52 days, and even the enemies could see that God had helped them; they became afraid and lost their confidence. When courage is undergirded by trust in God and obedience to God, others will notice, because it is not self-made bravery. It’s the same for us today. When the work God has given you faces obstacles, and people pressure you to quit, hide, or compromise, don’t give up and don’t give in. Pray to God, trust that He is fighting for you, and stay in the obedience lane.
days.upward:
Nehemiah looked to God before he looked at the enemies.
He prayed first. He remembered God’s promises. He trusted that “the good hand of my God was upon me.”
Courage that obeys God rather than man starts here.
God has given a work. God’s voice is higher than the voices that mock, threaten, or invite you to come down.
upward_questions: When pressure comes, do you look first at the people who want you to stop—or at the God who called you to the work?
days.inward:
This courage lives in the heart.
Fear says, “Get off the wall. Hide. Make it easier.”
Pride says, “Prove yourself.”
Nehemiah did neither. He stayed faithful.
Godly courage chooses obedience even when it costs reputation, comfort, or safety.
The question inside becomes: “Will I come down, or will I keep doing what God asked?”
inward_questions: Where do you feel most tempted to “come down” from what you know is right?
What fear usually tries to pull you away?
days.outward:
Nehemiah’s obedience was public and practical.
He kept building. He posted guards. He would not meet the enemy on their terms. He would not pretend to be holy by hiding in the temple.
This courage looks like staying in the work God has given:
telling the truth, keeping a commitment, refusing a compromise, or standing with God’s people when it would be easier to walk away.
outward_questions: Is there one place this week where obeying God means staying with the work instead of coming down?
days.prayer:
God, You gave Nehemiah a work and the courage not to leave it.
When people mock, threaten, or invite me to quit, help me obey You rather than them.
Keep me on the wall.
Let Your good hand be upon me. Amen.
self_application: What “wall” has God given me to keep building right now—a hard obedience, a true word, a faithful habit, or a stand I do not want to leave?
Who or what is trying to get me to come down?
What would it look like to stay at the work this week?
days.love_in_action: Choose one small act of courage that shows love and obedience today: stay faithful to the work God has given, refuse to come down when pressured, encourage someone who is tired of building, or keep doing what is right when mockery makes it hard.
love_in_action_questions: What is one small courageous step I can take this week, choosing to obey God rather than come down?

days.title: Courage That Speaks Truth Under Pressure
days.scripture_text:
When they saw the courage of Peter and John and realized that they were unschooled, ordinary men, they were astonished and they took note that these men had been with Jesus.

But Peter and John replied, “Which is right in God’s eyes: to listen to you, or to him? You be the judges! As for us, we cannot help speaking about what we have seen and heard.”
days.context:
Peter and John had just healed a man who could not walk. A crowd gathered, and they began teaching them about the risen Jesus.
Those who believed in Jesus grew to about 5,000.
The powerful religious leaders were angry and furious. Weeks before, they had crucified Jesus.
They arrested Peter and John and ordered them to stop speaking in Jesus’ name.

The leaders noticed something they could not explain:
“They saw the courage of Peter and John.” (Acts 4:13)
The Greek word translated “courage” or “boldness” is more than just being brave.
It’s fearless speech—holding back nothing even when there are costs involved.
In the book of Acts this courage is tied to speaking about Jesus and being filled with the Spirit.
The apostles prayed for boldness (courage) to speak truth:
“Now, Lord, consider their threats and enable your servants to speak your word with great boldness.” (Acts 4:29)

The leaders also noticed another thing:
“They took note that these men had been with Jesus.” (Acts 4:13)
Courage under pressure is not self-generated; it is the outcome of being in close relationship with Jesus.

The leaders commanded the apostles to stop speaking or teaching about Jesus.
Peter and John answered:
“Which is right in God’s eyes: to listen to you, or to him? You be the judges! As for us, we cannot help speaking about what we have seen and heard.” (Acts 4:19-20)
They refused to stay silent.
Speaking truth about Jesus mattered more than safety or approval.
days.deeper_text:
The priests and the captain of the temple guard and the Sadducees came up to Peter and John while they were speaking to the people. They were greatly disturbed because the apostles were teaching the people, proclaiming in Jesus the resurrection of the dead. They seized Peter and John and, because it was evening, they put them in jail until the next day. But many who heard the message believed; so the number of men who believed grew to about five thousand.

The next day the rulers, the elders and the teachers of the law met in Jerusalem. Annas the high priest was there, and so were Caiaphas, John, Alexander and others of the high priest’s family. They had Peter and John brought before them and began to question them: “By what power or what name did you do this?”

Then Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, said to them: “Rulers and elders of the people! If we are being called to account today for an act of kindness shown to a man who was lame and are being asked how he was healed, then know this, you and all the people of Israel: It is by the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom you crucified but whom God raised from the dead, that this man stands before you healed. Jesus is ‘the stone you builders rejected, which has become the cornerstone.’ Salvation is found in no one else, for there is no other name under heaven given to mankind by which we must be saved.”

When they saw the courage of Peter and John and realized that they were unschooled, ordinary men, they were astonished and they took note that these men had been with Jesus. But since they could see the man who had been healed standing there with them, there was nothing they could say. So they ordered them to withdraw from the Sanhedrin and then conferred together. “What are we going to do with these men?” they asked. “Everyone living in Jerusalem knows they have performed a notable sign, and we cannot deny it. But to stop this thing from spreading any further among the people, we must warn them to speak no longer to anyone in this name.”

Then they called them in again and commanded them not to speak or teach at all in the name of Jesus. But Peter and John replied, “Which is right in God’s eyes: to listen to you, or to him? You be the judges! As for us, we cannot help speaking about what we have seen and heard.”
days.summary: Peter and John had healed a man and spoken publicly about Jesus. The religious leaders arrested them and ordered them to stop teaching in His name. These religious leaders had killed Jesus just weeks before. The message of the apostles contradicted their verdict on Jesus, and this made them angry. The leaders saw their boldness (courage) and recognized that they had been with Jesus. Peter and John refused to stay silent. They said they could not stop speaking the truth about Jesus, about what they had seen and heard. They were eyewitnesses to the testimony of Jesus: Son of God, risen from the dead, rejected and killed by the leaders, the only One who saves. Their courage to speak God’s truth, even when the audience was powerful and hostile, was the byproduct of their close relationship with Jesus and empowered by the Holy Spirit.
days.upward:
Courage that speaks truth starts by looking to God.
When pressure rises to stay quiet, the real question is not “What will people think if I speak?”
It is “What has God made known, and how do I honor Him?”
Peter and John spoke because they had seen and heard the truth about Jesus. Their loyalty was to God first.
upward_questions: When truth needs to be spoken, whose opinion weighs more in your heart—God’s or the people around you?
days.inward:
This courage begins inside.
Fear of rejection, embarrassment, or conflict can make us stay silent even when we know the truth.
God invites a deeper honesty in the heart: a willingness to value truth more than comfort.
inward_questions: Where do you feel the strongest pull to stay quiet when you know you should speak?
What fear usually holds you back?
days.outward:
Speaking truth under pressure shows up in real moments.
It may mean gently correcting a false idea, refusing to laugh at what is wrong, or saying what is true about Jesus even when it feels risky.
Peter and John did not shout to win an argument. They simply refused to be silent about what God had done.
outward_questions: Is there one place in your life right now where staying silent feels safer than speaking truth?
days.prayer:
God, You are the God of truth.
When pressure tells me to stay quiet, give me courage to speak what is true.
Help me honor You more than the approval of people.
Make my words faithful and kind. Amen.
self_application: Where do I feel pressure to stay silent about what is true?
What is one clear truth God has shown me that I need to speak or live out?
If I chose to speak truth in that place, what might it cost—and what would it honor?
days.love_in_action: Choose one small act of courage that shows love and truth today: speak truth kindly, refuse to stay silent when something false is said, encourage someone standing alone, or stay faithful when it would be easier to go along.
love_in_action_questions: What is one small courageous step I can take this week, choosing to speak truth under pressure?

days.title: Courage That Endures Suffering and Trials
days.scripture_text: Not only so, but we also glory in our sufferings, because we know that suffering produces perseverance; perseverance, character; and character, hope. And hope does not put us to shame, because God’s love has been poured out into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us.
days.context:
The first Christians paid a real price for following Jesus.
Some were publicly shamed. Some were put in prison. Some lost their property. Some suffered physical violence.
The hardship was not just one day. It kept coming.

Paul’s testimony is the best evidence.
He was beaten, stoned and left for dead, five times received lashes, shipwrecked, imprisoned, went without food and sleep, abandoned.
God did not treat their suffering as wasted.

Paul shows a chain of what God can form through it:
Suffering → Perseverance → Proven Character → Hope
Each link depends on the one before it.
Without suffering you can’t get perseverance, proven character, and hope.

• Suffering — the word means to squeeze or press together: being crushed under a weight, pressed from all sides.
• Perseverance — the strength to bear up under pressure. It’s not self-made toughness. It’s an active strength God gives. Think of Paul’s runner metaphor: not quitting, even when the body wants to, until the finish line.
• Character — character proven genuine, certified as approved after testing, like metal refined in fire.
• Hope — to anticipate what is sure or certain; trust in God and His future promises with joy. This is evidence from personal experience.

This courage is not the absence of fear.
It’s a received God-strength to stay faithful when the easy way would mean quitting.
Courage is not a “solo” act but is shared in community with other believers.
days.deeper_text: Therefore, since we have been justified through faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have gained access by faith into this grace in which we now stand. And we boast in the hope of the glory of God. Not only so, but we also glory in our sufferings, because we know that suffering produces perseverance; perseverance, character; and character, hope. And hope does not put us to shame, because God’s love has been poured out into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us.
days.summary: Paul starts with our standing in Christ—peace with God and hope of the glory of God. In the Old Testament, the Hebrew word for glory (kabod) carries the idea of “weight” or “heaviness.” God’s glory is the weightiest thing that exists. Then Paul turns to suffering. He says we boast in the hope of the glory of God and in our sufferings—“boast” and “glory” translate the same Greek word. So how can we boast in our sufferings when the world says “not fair” or points to victimhood? We can boast in our sufferings because of our eternal perspective: God uses our suffering to strengthen our faith in Him and to form Christlike character in us. This perspective moves us to have the courage to act despite fear. This courage is supernatural, not self-made, because, as Paul says, suffering can produce perseverance, perseverance can produce proven character, and proven character can produce hope. That hope does not disappoint, because it is held by God’s poured-out love. Hard seasons are not wasted. They can form a steadiness that comfort never could. This means a failed test, a broken friendship, anxiety about the future, or pressure to compromise is not the last word. God can use the trial to build perseverance, character, and a hope anchored in His love.
days.upward:
Enduring courage starts by looking to God, not by trying to make yourself brave.
Hard seasons are not always random. God can use them to forge something in you.
It’s the same pressure the early Christians experienced, just different in form.
Hope does not rest on circumstances.
It rests on this: God’s love has been poured into our hearts.

• Look back: God has been faithful before.
• Look up: His love is being given. His strength is being given.
• Look forward: This hope will not put you to shame.

What God wants you to have is Christlike character, which cannot be produced by a comfortable life.
Courage is knowing you are not alone.
Courage is knowing God is with you in the hard places.
upward_questions: When something hard persists, do you try to manufacture courage—or look to the God who pours out His love?
days.inward:
This God-given courage lives in our hearts.
Fear, failure, anxiety, and weariness can make you want to quit.
God’s Word does not say, “Get back to easy.”
It says that suffering can produce perseverance, perseverance can produce proven character, and proven character can produce hope.

If you are struggling with school, friendship, family, relationships, or a sense that you are failing, hear this:
In God’s hands the pain is not wasted. It’s productive. God is bringing something out of you through the squeezing.
“In that hard place, I chose to trust God, and I’m still standing because God is holding me.” That is proven character, and it makes hope in God real.
inward_questions: Where do you feel most tempted to take the easy way out?
What might God be forming in you if you stay faithful there: perseverance, character, or hope?
days.outward:
Courage shows up in everyday life.
• Stay honest when lying is easier.
• Stay kind when you are tired.
• Choose to forgive rather than being angry or bitter.
• Refuse to compromise God’s truth to keep approval.
• Keep following Jesus when others drift.
Everyday faithfulness is still courage.
It is doing what is right and true while God forms a hope that circumstances cannot destroy.
outward_questions: Is there one place where staying faithful to God’s truth would cost you comfort, image, or acceptance?
days.prayer:
God, You see the hard things that do not end quickly.
I need the courage that You give.
Pour Your love into my heart.
Use suffering to form perseverance, character, and hope in me.
Help me stay faithful when the easy way would mean giving up. Amen.
self_application: Where do I feel worn down by a hard season that has lasted too long?
What would it look like to receive courage from God there, instead of trying to be tough on my own?
If I stayed faithful this week, what link in the chain might God be forming: perseverance, proven character, or hope?
days.love_in_action: Choose one small act of courage that shows love and endurance today: stay faithful when it would be easier to compromise, encourage someone who is weary, keep doing what is right when it is tiring, or remain kind when it would be easier to quit.
love_in_action_questions: What is one small courageous step I can take this week, choosing God’s truth over the easy way?

days.title: Courage Empowered by the Holy Spirit
days.scripture_text: For the Spirit God gave us does not make us timid, but gives us power, love and self-discipline.

days.context:
Emperor Nero was persecuting Christians in Rome. Paul wrote to Timothy from prison (a Roman dungeon). He was awaiting his execution for speaking about Jesus. He knew the cost.
Paul was a mentor to Timothy.

Timothy was young and leading a difficult church in Ephesus—a city steeped in pagan cults.
There were aggressive false teachers in the church corrupting the minds of the people.
Paul told Timothy what to do: 1) order these men to stop the false teaching, and 2) bring people back to the truth by teaching God’s truth.
Timothy was already facing intimidation because of his young age.
He was struggling and timid in the face of pressure and opposition.
Confronting combative false teachers made Timothy fearful, and he shrank back.

Paul knew this. He didn’t tell Timothy to pick himself up and be brave.
He told Timothy that he already had what he needed to confront them.
Paul reminded Timothy that the Spirit of God who is in him “does not make us timid.”
He told Timothy how to do it: power, love and self-discipline.
These three gifts from the Holy Spirit are to be used together.
• Power gave Timothy supernatural ability to confront aggressive, malicious, and hostile false teachers.
• Love gave Timothy sacrificial and selfless service to God and others—speaking truth in love.
• Self-discipline gave Timothy self-control—level-headedness—over his emotions and actions.

Courage is not the absence of fear.
God-given courage is grounded in God’s strength and presence in the face of fear.
Paul’s own life was the example: courage in the face of death.
He was beaten, jailed, and often weak. He still spoke and endured—not by might, and not by his own nerve, but by the Spirit of God.
days.deeper_text:
“For this reason I remind you to fan into flame the gift of God, which is in you through the laying on of my hands, for God gave us a spirit not of fear but of power and love and self-control. Therefore do not be ashamed of the testimony about our Lord, nor of me his prisoner, but share in suffering for the gospel by the power of God.” (2 Timothy 1:6-8)

“For this reason I bow my knees before the Father… that according to the riches of his glory he may grant you to be strengthened with power through his Spirit in your inner being, so that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith.” (Ephesians 3:14, 16-17)
days.summary: Paul wrote these words as a man who had suffered for Christ. He told Timothy that God does not give a spirit of fear. He gives power, love, and self-control. That gift is meant to be fanned into flame, not hidden. In Ephesians, Paul prays that God would strengthen believers with power through the Holy Spirit in the inner being, so that Christ would dwell in their hearts. The meaning is this: biblical courage is supernatural. It is God strengthening a person from the inside so they can obey on the outside. Paul is the example. He was weak, imprisoned, and often afraid of the cost—and still he depended on the Spirit, not on himself. For youth, this means you do not have to invent bravery. Ask God to strengthen your inner being. Those who belong to Jesus are not left alone in their fear. And for those still deciding about Jesus, the first Spirit-given step is to turn to Him.
days.upward:
Spirit-empowered courage starts by looking to God, not by digging deeper into yourself.
Paul says God gave this spirit. It is a gift.
Ephesians 3:16 says the strength comes through His Spirit in your inner being. God works from the inside out.
When fear rises, the first move is not “I have to be braver.”
It is “God, strengthen me by Your Spirit.”
upward_questions: When you feel afraid, do you first try to pump yourself up—or ask God to strengthen you from the inside?
days.inward:
This courage begins in the heart.
2 Timothy 1:7 names three things God gives instead of fear:
• power — strength to do what you cannot do alone
• love — a heart that moves toward God and others, not only toward self-protection
• self-control — a steady mind that does not let fear run the whole person
Paul knew fear and weakness. He still asked God to strengthen the inner being.
That is where true courage is formed.

If you have trusted Jesus, you are not left to face pressure alone.
If you have not yet trusted Him, the first courageous step is not pretending you already have this power. It is turning to Him.
inward_questions: Where does fear usually live in you—silence, people-pleasing, or holding back from Jesus Himself?
Which gift do you need most right now: power, love, or self-control?
days.outward:
Paul did not stay brave only in private.
He preached, wrote, suffered, and asked others to pray that he would keep speaking with boldness—even in chains.
Spirit-given courage shows up in real obedience:
tell the truth about Jesus, refuse to hide your faith, stay kind under pressure, or take the next faithful step when fear says stop.
outward_questions: Is there one place where you know what is true, but fear is keeping you silent or still?
days.prayer:
God, You did not give a spirit of fear.
Strengthen me with power through Your Spirit in my inner being.
Give me power, love, and self-control.
Help me obey You with boldness, as You helped Paul. Amen.
self_application: Where do I feel most powerless to be faithful?
Have I been trying to create courage on my own?
What is one place I need to ask God for Spirit-given power, love, and self-control this week?
days.love_in_action: Choose one small act of courage that depends on God, not on your own strength: speak truth about Jesus kindly, refuse to hide your faith, encourage someone who is afraid, or take the next obedient step when it would be easier to stay quiet.
love_in_action_questions: What is one small courageous step I can take this week, asking God to give the boldness I do not have on my own?
